tool_selection.reasoning: SHAP provides robust, model-agnostic feature importance scores that can identify which features drive predictions in misclassified instances. LIME and Integrated Gradients offer local interpretability to validate how specific features contribute to the prediction. Sensitivity analysis directly tests the effect of removing a feature, helping isolate spurious correlations. Using all together ensures both global and local insight into shared spurious patterns, especially when ground truth is unknown and the model is misclassifying all instances.

However, the model misinterprets this low, stable value as a malignancy indicator due to spurious correlation with training data distribution.
explanation.explanation: The model assigns high importance to mean symmetry because it is consistently low in benign cases and appears to be misclassified as a malignancy signal. Despite its semantic alignment with benign morphology, the model has learned to associate low symmetry values with malignancy, creating a spurious pattern that leads to false positives. This over-penalization of low symmetry values, even when they are consistent with benign characteristics, causes the misclassification.

reasoning.query: Evaluate whether any shared features (e.g., mean smoothness, mean concavity) are semantically plausible in relation to malignancy and whether they might be acting as spurious predictors due to correlation with class distributions.

result.explanation: The misclassified instances (541 and 291) are both benign in truth but predicted as malignant with moderate confidence (70.33%). The shared features showing notable differences are those related to texture and shape complexity: mean smoothness, mean compactness, mean concavity, mean concave points, and mean fractal dimension. These features are semantically plausible in cancer classification as they reflect cellular structure — smoother, more compact, or less irregular shapes are typically associated with benign tumors. However, in these cases, the values (e.g., mean smoothness ≈ 0.088–0.090, mean concavity ≈ 0.059–0.101) are within the lower range consistent with benign cases. The model’s misprediction likely stems from a spurious correlation: these features are highly correlated with class distribution in training data, where benign samples tend to have lower compactness and concavity, and the model has learned to over-penalize low values as indicative of malignancy. This creates a spurious pattern where low values in these features are misinterpreted as malignancy indicators, even though they are semantically aligned with benignity. Thus, these features are semantically related to tumor morphology but may serve as spurious predictors due to strong statistical correlation with class distribution in training data.
